title: Λέων καὶ λαγωός
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 204. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Λέων περιτυχὼν λαγωῷ κοιμωμένῳ, τοῦτον ἔμελλε καταφαγεῖν· μεταξὺ δὲ θεασάμενος ἔλαφον παριοῦσαν, ἀφεὶς τὸν λαγωόν, ἐκείνην ἐδίωκεν.
sentences.tr: Leōn peritychōn lagōōi koimōmenōi, touton emelle kataphagein· metaxy de theasamenos elaphon pariousan, apheis ton lagōon, ekeinēn ediōken.
sentences.l: A lion, having come upon a hare sleeping, was about to devour him ; but meanwhile, having caught sight of a deer going past, having let the hare go, he pursued her.
sentences.i: A lion came upon a hare asleep and was on the point of eating him ; but meanwhile he caught sight of a deer going by, and, letting the hare go, gave chase to her.
sentences.n: The chain of aorist participles is the fable's engine: each one clears a step and the finite verb carries the point. The deer is feminine here (παριοῦσαν, ἐκείνην); ἔλαφος serves for either sex.

sentences.t: Ὁ μὲν οὖν παρὰ τὸν ψόφον ἐξαναστὰς ἔφυγεν.
sentences.tr: Ho men oun para ton psophon exanastas ephygen.
sentences.l: So the one, having started up at the noise, fled.
sentences.i: The hare, then, started up at the noise and fled.
sentences.n: παρά with the accusative here marks the occasion, 'at the noise'. ὁ μέν sets up the ὁ δέ that opens the next sentence: first the hare's part of the outcome, then the lion's.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ λέων ἐπὶ πολὺ διώξας τὴν ἔλαφον, ἐπειδὴ καταλαβεῖν οὐκ ἠδυνήθη, ἐπανῆλθεν ἐπὶ τὸν λαγωόν· εὑρὼν δὲ καὶ αὐτὸν πεφευγότα ἔφη· « Ἀλλ’ ἐγὼ δίκαια πέπονθα, ὅτι ἀφεὶς τὴν ἐν χερσὶ βοράν, ἐλπίδα μείζονα προέκρινα. »
sentences.tr: Ho de leōn epi poly diōxas tēn elaphon, epeidē katalabein ouk ēdynēthē, epanēlthen epi ton lagōon· heurōn de kai auton pepheugota ephē· « All’ egō dikaia pepontha, hoti apheis tēn en chersi boran, elpida meizona proekrina. »
sentences.l: And the lion, having chased the deer a long way, since he was not able to catch her, came back to the hare ; but finding that he too had fled, he said: « Well, I have suffered just things, because, having let go the food in my hands, I gave the preference to a greater hope. »
sentences.i: The lion chased the deer a long way, and when he could not catch her, came back to the hare ; but finding that he too had gone, he said: « I have suffered no more than I deserved: I let go the food already in my hands and gave the preference to a bigger hope. »
sentences.n: πεφευγότα is a supplementary participle after εὑρών — the perfect states the standing result: not 'saw him fleeing' but 'found that he was gone'. δίκαια πέπονθα, 'I have suffered just things', is a standing Greek idiom for having got exactly what one deserved. τὴν ἐν χερσὶ βοράν is the article carrying a whole phrase, 'the in-the-hands food', and the epimythium picks it up again.

sentences.t: Οὕτως ἔνιοι τῶν ἀνθρώπων μετρίοις κέρδεσι μὴ ἀρκούμενοι, μείζονας δὲ ἐλπίδας διώκοντες λανθάνουσι καὶ τὰ ἐν χερσὶ προϊέμενοι.
sentences.tr: Houtōs enioi tōn anthrōpōn metriois kerdesi mē arkoumenoi, meizonas de elpidas diōkontes lanthanousi kai ta en chersi proiemenoi.
sentences.l: Thus some among men, not being content with moderate gains, but chasing greater hopes, escape their own notice letting go even what is in their hands.
sentences.i: Thus some men, not content with moderate gains but chasing greater hopes, let go even what they already hold without noticing that they are doing it.
sentences.n: λανθάνω with a supplementary participle puts the action in the participle and the unawareness in the verb: they let go, and it is the letting-go that escapes them. ἀρκέομαι takes the dative of what one is content with.
